_about: Prewritten bedtime stories. Placeholders: {name}; pronouns {they} {them} {their} {theirs} {themself} (capitalize the first letter for the start of a sentence: {They}); verbs that follow the pronoun as [was|were] (she/he form first, they form second); {person} and {person2} for special people; {pet} and {pet_kind}. A paragraph that starts with [pet] is left out when the child has no pet. Each story uses its three Spark Words at least three times. approved: false until the founder has read it.

stories.title: {name} and the Fossil in the Garden
stories.beforeQuestion: The story is called "{name} and the Fossil in the Garden." What do you think {name} might find?
stories.talkQuestion: Why do you think {name} felt a little bit sad and a little bit lucky when {they} remembered that dinosaurs are extinct? How would you feel?
paragraphs: It was the first warm Saturday of spring, and {name} was helping {person} dig in the garden. The soil was dark and soft, and it smelled like rain. {name} had a little blue shovel, a bucket, and a very big feeling that something exciting was about to happen.
[pet] {pet} the {pet_kind} was helping too, in {pet}'s own way. Mostly that meant sniffing every hole and sitting right where {name} wanted to dig next.
"What are we planting?" {name} asked. "Carrots," said {person}, "and sunflowers, if we are lucky." {name} pushed the shovel down, and it went clunk. Not a soft, soily sound. A hard, stony clunk.

{name} brushed the dirt away with careful fingers. Under the soil was a flat grey stone, and pressed into the stone was a curly shape, like a snail shell made of rock. "{person}!" {name} whispered. "I think I found a fossil!"

{person} knelt down and looked very closely. "You did," {person} said. "A fossil is what is left when something lived a long, long time ago, and its shape slowly turned into stone. This little shell might be older than the dinosaurs."
{name}'s eyes went wide. Older than the dinosaurs! {They} held the fossil up to the sun and turned it slowly. It felt cool and heavy and secret, as if it had been waiting just for {them}.

That night, {name} could not stop thinking about it. {They} put the fossil on the windowsill, where the moon could see it, and climbed into bed. And just as {their} eyes were closing, the fossil began to glow.

At first it was only a faint, silvery light. Then the light grew, and grew, until it filled the whole room, and {name} was not in bed any more. {They} [was|were] standing in a forest of enormous ferns, taller than a house, with leaves as big as umbrellas.
The air was warm and damp and buzzing with dragonflies. Somewhere far off, something went thud. Then thud again, closer. The ground gave a little shiver under {name}'s feet.

{name} peeked between two giant leaves. A line of shiny beetles marched past, each one as big as a shoe. A bird with a long, toothy beak flapped overhead and called, "Kraa! Kraa!" Everything here was bigger, louder and greener than anything {name} had ever seen.

Through the ferns came the most enormous animal {name} had ever seen. It had a long, long neck, a long, long tail, and a kind face way up high, chewing slowly on a mouthful of leaves. It was a dinosaur, and it was looking right at {them}.

"Hello," said {name}, in {their} bravest voice. The dinosaur blinked its big brown eyes. Then it lowered its enormous head, all the way down, until its nose was right in front of {name}, and it gave a soft, warm snuffle that smelled like salad.

{name} laughed. "I found your fossil friend," {they} said, and held out {their} hand. There, in {their} palm, was the curly stone shell from the garden. The dinosaur sniffed it, and its tail swished happily through the ferns.
[pet] And who should come bounding through the ferns but {pet}! Even here, in a time long, long ago, {pet} was right by {name}'s side, sniffing the giant dinosaur footprints with great interest.

The dinosaur bent its long neck, and {name} understood. {They} climbed up onto its back, holding on carefully, and the dinosaur began to walk. Thud, thud, thud. From up high, {name} could see a lake that sparkled like glass, a family of little dinosaurs splashing at the edge, and a volcano far away, puffing a sleepy grey cloud.

They stopped by the lake for a drink. The water was so clear that {name} could see little fish darting between the stones, and a long, flat footprint pressed into the mud at the edge. {name} put {their} own foot beside it. The footprint was bigger than {their} whole bed!

"Will there be dinosaurs forever?" {name} asked. The dinosaur did not answer, but {name} remembered what {person} had said. Dinosaurs are extinct. That means there are none left alive anywhere in the world. They lived so long ago that all we have now are their bones, their footprints and their fossils.
It made {name} feel a little bit sad, and a little bit lucky. Extinct meant {they} could never meet a real dinosaur. But here {they} [was|were], riding on one, in a dream that felt very real indeed.
"I will remember you," {name} told the dinosaur, patting its enormous neck. "Even if you are extinct, I will tell everyone about you."

The dinosaur hummed a low, rumbly hum, the kind you feel in your tummy more than you hear with your ears. Then it walked slowly back through the ferns, to the place where {name} had first arrived. The silvery light was there again, glowing softly between the leaves.

{name} slid down the dinosaur's tail like a slide. Whee! {They} landed on soft moss and turned to wave goodbye. The dinosaur lowered its head one last time and gave {name}'s hair a gentle, salady snuffle.
Then the light grew bright, and warm, and {name} closed {their} eyes.

When {they} opened them again, {they} [was|were] back in {their} own bed. The moon was shining through the window. The fossil sat on the windowsill, just a quiet grey stone with a curly shape inside, the way it had always been.
[pet] {pet} was curled up at the foot of the bed, snoring softly, with one paw twitching as if {pet} were still running through the ferns.

{name} smiled a sleepy smile. In the morning, {they} would tell {person} everything: the enormous ferns, the friendly dinosaur, the ride by the sparkling lake. {person} might say it was only a dream. But {name} would know it was something even better: a story that started with a fossil in the garden.
{name} pulled the blanket up to {their} chin. Outside, the garden was quiet. Somewhere under the soil, maybe, there were more fossils waiting to be found, and more stories from long, long ago.
{name} thought about the dinosaur's warm, salady snuffle and laughed softly into {their} pillow.
And with that happy thought, {name} drifted off to sleep.

stories.title: {name} and the Distant Star
stories.beforeQuestion: The story is called "{name} and the Distant Star." Where do you think {name} might go?
stories.talkQuestion: The star said it was never really alone. Why do you think it felt that way? Who do you think about when you look up at the sky?
paragraphs: Every night before bed, {name} and {person} had a special job. They went out to the back porch, wrapped up in a blanket, and said goodnight to the sky.
Tonight the sky was very clear. The moon was a thin silver smile, and the stars were coming out one by one, as if someone were switching on tiny lights.
[pet] {pet} the {pet_kind} came too, of course. {pet} sat on the porch step, looking up as if {pet} were counting the stars as well.
"Look," said {person}, pointing. "Do you see that little glimmer, just above the big tree?" {name} looked. There it was: one small light, blinking softly, as if it were winking.
"That is a star," said {person}. "It is very, very distant. It is so far away that its light has been travelling for years and years just to reach your eyes tonight."
{name} thought about that. Years and years! That little glimmer of light had started its trip before {name} was even born, and now here it was, right on time, saying hello.

"How far is distant?" {name} asked. {person} laughed. "Farther than the grocery store. Farther than the beach. Farther than the moon. If you drove a car there, you would have to drive for millions of years, and you would need a lot of snacks."
"What do stars do all night?" {name} asked. "They shine," said {person}. "That is their job, the way your job is to grow and play and dream."
{name} giggled, but {they} kept looking at the star. It looked lonely up there, all by itself. "I wish I could visit it," {they} said.
That night, tucked into bed, {name} looked out the window. The distant star was still there, glimmering above the tree. {name} whispered, "Goodnight, star," and closed {their} eyes.
And then the strangest, most wonderful thing happened. {name}'s bed began to float. Up it went, gently, past the window, past the big tree, up and up into the dark blue sky.
{name} held on to {their} pillow and peeked over the edge. There was the house, getting smaller. There was the street, and the park, and the whole sleepy town, twinkling with porch lights.
[pet] {pet} was riding along too, sitting at the end of the bed with {pet}'s ears blowing in the breeze, looking as calm as if beds flew every night.
The bed floated higher and higher, until the whole round Earth was below, blue and green and swirled with white clouds. And around the Earth went the moon, slowly and steadily, in a big circle.

From up here, {name} could see the oceans shining, the mountains like crumpled paper, and the long, bright line where night meets morning on the other side of the world. It was so quiet that {name} could hear {their} own heart, beating slow and steady.

"The moon is going around and around," said {name}. A soft voice answered, "That is called an orbit." {name} turned. Floating beside the bed was a small, friendly light, shaped a little like a star and a little like a smile.
"I am the star you said goodnight to," the light said. "I heard you. Nobody has said goodnight to me in a very long time."
{name} beamed. "You came all the way from your distant home?" "Just for a visit," said the star. "Would you like to see how an orbit works?"
{name} nodded so hard that {their} hair bounced. The star twirled, and the bed began to move in a big, slow circle around the moon. Around and around they went, smooth as a merry-go-round.
"We are in orbit!" {name} laughed. "Just like the moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth goes around the sun," said the star. "Everything up here is dancing in circles."

As they went around, the star told {name} wonderful things. About planets with rings like hula hoops. About a red planet with mountains taller than any on Earth. About clouds of stardust, glimmering in every colour, where brand-new stars are born.
The star showed {name} a comet, too, zooming past with a long, sparkly tail like a kite string made of light. {name} waved, and the comet seemed to wave its tail back.
Then the star told {name} a secret. "When you feel far from someone you love, look up. The same moon shines on both of you." {name} thought of {person}, asleep downstairs, and felt warm all over.

"Is it ever lonely, being so far away?" {name} asked. The star thought for a moment. "Sometimes," it said. "But every night, someone looks up. And every night, my light reaches them. So I am never really alone."
{name} liked that very much.
After one more slow orbit around the moon, the star gave a sparkly yawn. "It is time for us both to rest," it said. "I have to shine tomorrow, and you have to grow."
{name} gave the star a careful hug. It felt like hugging a warm mug of cocoa, cosy and bright.
The bed began to float down, gently, gently, through the clouds, past the sleepy town, past the big tree, and in through the window, landing with the softest little bump.
[pet] {pet} hopped down, turned around three times, and curled up on the rug with a long, happy sigh.
{name} snuggled under the blanket. Outside, above the big tree, the distant star gave one last glimmer, like a wink. "Goodnight, star," {name} whispered. "Goodnight, {name}," the light seemed to say.
Tomorrow night, {name} would tell {person} all about the orbit, the planets with rings and the friendly little star. But for now, {they} [was|were] warm and cosy and very, very sleepy.
{name} thought about the distant star, still shining high above the house, keeping watch over the whole sleepy town.
And as the Earth turned slowly in its orbit, carrying {name} gently through the night, {name} fell fast asleep.
